96 Plus, Anthropic’s AI vision, chatbots do econ data, and Kevin Warsh’s global audience   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   Interest Rates Look Kinda Low   Plus, Anthropic’s AI vision, chatbots do econ data, and Kevin Warsh’s global audience   You’ve heard the reasons the Fed will probably raise rates, if not this week then sometime soon: the inflationary effects of the AI investment boom and the Iran war energy crunch.

   There is another critical factor you may not have considered: Interest rates are, simply, low. For now, and for the foreseeable future, rates at today’s level or higher should be considered normal.

   You might ask, low relative to what? Theoretically, there is a “neutral” interest rate that keeps growth, unemployment and inflation steady, like the optimal thermostat setting that keeps your house comfortable. Over the long run, rates should average around neutral.

   In September, the median Fed official thought the fed-funds rate would be 3.2% over the long run, well below its current setting of 3.75% to 4%. That is why many Fed officials had described rates as “restrictive,” i.e., holding back demand and price pressure.

   But neutral can’t really be observed. It must be inferred from the economy and markets, and neither is behaving as if rates are restrictive: Growth is solid, stocks are near a record, and big speculative companies like Anthropic are raising billions of dollars.

   One way to measure neutral is to ask where markets think rates will be for the next 10 years. A popular model developed by economists Tobias Adrian, Richard Crump and Emanuel Moench (known as the ACM model, for short) and maintained by the New York Fed divides a 10-year bond yield into expected short-term rates over the next decade and a “term premium,” the extra return investors demand to lock up their money for years instead of weeks.

         With the usual caveat that models are imprecise, this one as of last week said markets think short-term rates will average 4.3% over the next decade, which implies today’s rates are relatively low. 

   Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has played down “neutral” as a useful concept but has said financial conditions don’t look restrictive, implying he is comfortable raising rates further. 

   This will disappoint borrowers hoping for a big drop in rates once inflation and oil recede. The good news is that a higher normal for rates points to a higher normal for economic growth, too.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter , your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics.   If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       What I’m Following   Ahead of its planned IPO next month, Anthropic’s prospectus lays out a sweeping vision for how AI will transform the economy . The technology’s economic impact will be greater than that of “industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet,” the company writes. The prospectus says little about the risk that AI could disrupt the labor market and boost unemployment, but acknowledges that the technology could concentrate power and wealth. It is worth remembering the document is intended to sell shares.

   Meanwhile, Harvard economist Jason Furman used AI to code a website, Econvitals, that analyzes the latest econ data . Furman says he vibe-coded the initial version of the website in one evening this spring, but that even working with chatbots, it took plenty of hands-on work: “I feel like the person who said, ‘I didn’t do it because it was easy but because I thought it would be easy.’” Without coding agents, the project would have taken a team of 50 people working for three years on a budget of $20 million to complete. At least, that is what Claude—perhaps a bit self-servingly—told Furman.

   Some skepticism about consumers’ willingness to pay up for chatbots could be wise. Harvard’s Mark Egan and four co-authors find in a new paper that everyday users are highly price sensitive when buying chatbot subscriptions, and show little brand loyalty. As of April, less than 3% of Americans paid for an AI chatbot, with nearly all subscribing to basic plans costing less than $30 a month. Retention rates were between 20% and 45%, lower than for many other subscription products. Brand-switching picked up around the release of new models, showing that model companies risk losing revenue if they don’t stay at the bleeding edge.

   At his press conference this week, Warsh’s audience will stretch from Jacksonville to Jakarta , WSJ’s Nick Timiraos tells us: “Warsh’s push to say less is felt far beyond the U.S. When the Fed is hard to read, central banks abroad manage swings in their currencies and capital flows without a clear sense of what’s coming. ‘Fed communication right now is something that has become very closed,’ Destry Damayanti, governor of Indonesia’s central bank, told the Journal at the IMF meetings in Bangkok this month. People ‘really need to have clear news from a respected institution,’ she said.” On Wednesday, Warsh gets the microphone again. Read more of Nick’s coverage here .

       Subscriptions make our journalism possible. WSJ Economics readers can enjoy a special rate on a new subscription . If you’re already a WSJ subscriber, thank you for your support. 

       More From WSJ         • Manufacturers are hiring again, but the qualifications have changed : Factory opportunities skew much more toward management posts that require higher education, rather than the lower-skilled but high-paying factory jobs of yore.

   • A Princeton chemical engineering Ph.D. applied to 2,300 jobs and still can’t get one. His father is at a loss: “We never dreamed he would have issues. He’s an Eagle Scout, he helps others, he’s environmentally conscious, he’s physically fit. He’s smarter than I am, he’s more articulate than I am. He’s got an encyclopedic knowledge of history.”

   • Major companies deny that they are using AI or other technology to jack up prices based on individual customers’ behavior—but those denials have failed to stem many shoppers’ suspicions .

       What to Watch   Tuesday 

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: Orders for durable goods likely rose by 1.2% in September, economists estimate.

   • 10 a.m. ET: Forecasters expect that new home sales fell 4.2% month over month in September and that the Conference Board’s consumer-confidence index declined this month.

   Wednesday 

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: The government of U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to deliver its first annual budget, as concerns about rich countries’ fiscal trajectories deepen.

   • 2 p.m. ET: The Fed is expected to hold rates steady at 3.75% to 4%. Traders will watch Warsh’s press conference for clues about its next move in December.

   • 4 p.m. ET: Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet post quarterly earnings. Tech stocks struggled last week amid concerns the AI surge could prove a bubble.

       Reader Feedback   Thoughts on what you just read? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me.   

   Jonathan Steckloff, a student at Indiana University, responds to my note, “ Yes, the Fed Can Kill the AI Boom ”:  

   People forget about the opportunity cost of simply investing cash. Businesses like Meta and Alphabet used to be incredibly cash rich, but are deploying that cash into the AI build-out. If risk-free rates get high enough, the marginal temptation to return to the core business and simply invest excess cash increases. Pundits citing rates up on economic growth while also arguing higher rates pose no threat to the build-out miss the point. The premise of a higher neutral rate is that it brings savings and investment back into balance by encouraging saving and deterring investment at the margin. 

       What I’m Reading   • Persistent inflation owes to stubborn underlying trends—not just the one-off effects of tariffs and the Iran war. ( Matthew Klein )

   • A relief to the French government, Moody’s declined to downgrade the country’s debt, but said its decision assumed implementation of a deficit-reducing budget. ( Reuters )

Interest Rates Look Kinda Low
 
Plus, Anthropic’s AI vision, chatbots do econ data, and Kevin Warsh’s global audience
 

You’ve heard the reasons the Fed will probably raise rates, if not this week then sometime soon: the inflationary effects of the AI investment boom and the Iran war energy crunch.

 

There is another critical factor you may not have considered: Interest rates are, simply, low. For now, and for the foreseeable future, rates at today’s level or higher should be considered normal.

With the usual caveat that models are imprecise, this one as of last week said markets think short-term rates will average 4.3% over the next decade, which implies today’s rates are relatively low. 

 

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has played down “neutral” as a useful concept but has said financial conditions don’t look restrictive, implying he is comfortable raising rates further. 

 

This will disappoint borrowers hoping for a big drop in rates once inflation and oil recede. The good news is that a higher normal for rates points to a higher normal for economic growth, too.

What I’m Following

 

Ahead of its planned IPO next month, Anthropic’s prospectus lays out a sweeping vision for how AI will transform the economy. The technology’s economic impact will be greater than that of “industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet,” the company writes. The prospectus says little about the risk that AI could disrupt the labor market and boost unemployment, but acknowledges that the technology could concentrate power and wealth. It is worth remembering the document is intended to sell shares.

 

Meanwhile, Harvard economist Jason Furman used AI to code a website, Econvitals, that analyzes the latest econ data. Furman says he vibe-coded the initial version of the website in one evening this spring, but that even working with chatbots, it took plenty of hands-on work: “I feel like the person who said, ‘I didn’t do it because it was easy but because I thought it would be easy.’” Without coding agents, the project would have taken a team of 50 people working for three years on a budget of $20 million to complete. At least, that is what Claude—perhaps a bit self-servingly—told Furman.

 

Some skepticism about consumers’ willingness to pay up for chatbots could be wise. Harvard’s Mark Egan and four co-authors find in a new paper that everyday users are highly price sensitive when buying chatbot subscriptions, and show little brand loyalty. As of April, less than 3% of Americans paid for an AI chatbot, with nearly all subscribing to basic plans costing less than $30 a month. Retention rates were between 20% and 45%, lower than for many other subscription products. Brand-switching picked up around the release of new models, showing that model companies risk losing revenue if they don’t stay at the bleeding edge.

 

At his press conference this week, Warsh’s audience will stretch from Jacksonville to Jakarta, WSJ’s Nick Timiraos tells us: “Warsh’s push to say less is felt far beyond the U.S. When the Fed is hard to read, central banks abroad manage swings in their currencies and capital flows without a clear sense of what’s coming. ‘Fed communication right now is something that has become very closed,’ Destry Damayanti, governor of Indonesia’s central bank, told the Journal at the IMF meetings in Bangkok this month. People ‘really need to have clear news from a respected institution,’ she said.” On Wednesday, Warsh gets the microphone again. Read more of Nick’s coverage here.

More From WSJ

 
 
 
 

• Manufacturers are hiring again, but the qualifications have changed: Factory opportunities skew much more toward management posts that require higher education, rather than the lower-skilled but high-paying factory jobs of yore.

 

• A Princeton chemical engineering Ph.D. applied to 2,300 jobs and still can’t get one. His father is at a loss: “We never dreamed he would have issues. He’s an Eagle Scout, he helps others, he’s environmentally conscious, he’s physically fit. He’s smarter than I am, he’s more articulate than I am. He’s got an encyclopedic knowledge of history.”

Reader Feedback

 

Thoughts on what you just read? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me.  

 

Jonathan Steckloff, a student at Indiana University, responds to my note, “Yes, the Fed Can Kill the AI Boom”:  

 

People forget about the opportunity cost of simply investing cash. Businesses like Meta and Alphabet used to be incredibly cash rich, but are deploying that cash into the AI build-out. If risk-free rates get high enough, the marginal temptation to return to the core business and simply invest excess cash increases. Pundits citing rates up on economic growth while also arguing higher rates pose no threat to the build-out miss the point. The premise of a higher neutral rate is that it brings savings and investment back into balance by encouraging saving and deterring investment at the margin.
